title: Truth is like a precious stone
author: Crome, Samuel
summary: Built around a single Pope Francis quote — that truth offered in an open hand draws people in, while truth hurled at someone causes injury — this piece applies the metaphor directly to school leadership and the practice of giving feedback to staff. The author's core argument is that what changes the effect of a hard truth is never the truth itself but how it is handled: hurling it (reacting quickly out of impatience or fatigue, using incomplete evidence) causes damage, while holding it out with clarity, empathy, and sustained investment invites genuine collaboration and change. Three specific ingredients are named for 'holding the stone': clarity (clear, objective evidence rather than assumption), empathy (listening and being present to everyone's needs, not just delivering a verdict), and investment (walking alongside a colleague in the days after a hard conversation, not just during the meeting itself). The piece closes by explicitly naming the instinct leaders must resist under pressure — the urge to hurl the stone because it feels fast and decisive — arguing genuine improvement in a school culture comes from inviting staff into the process rather than throwing hard truths at people who are already tired.
points: The central metaphor, drawn from a Pope Francis quote, holds that truth held out openly draws people in while truth hurled at someone causes injury — the change is entirely in how it's handled, not the truth itself.

Three specific ingredients are named for 'holding the stone' well: clarity (objective evidence, not assumption or bias), empathy (being present to everyone's needs, not just delivering a verdict), and investment (ongoing follow-up, not just the initial conversation).

The urge to 'hurl' feedback is explicitly linked to leader fatigue and impatience for results, not to the accuracy of the truth being delivered, reframing self-control under pressure as the real leadership skill at stake.
Improvement is explicitly framed as a team effort requiring staff to feel invited into the process, rather than a leader delivering conclusions from above.

The piece closes with a direct rejection of confrontational leadership under pressure: 'we don't move forward by throwing hard truths at tired people. We lead them by opening our hands, inviting them to look closer, and building together.'
quotes: Truth is like a precious stone. Offer it in your hand, and it draws others to you; hurl it at someone, and it causes injury." Pope Francis
So, then, it is not the stone alone that is of note to others, but the way you offer it in your hand. Inviting participation.
What has changed is not the stone itself, but the way it is handled.

Hurling the stone is easy to do when we are busy, tired, or impatient for results. It's when we blaze in with all the answers, react too quickly to inaccurate or two-dimensional evidence, or forget to add the support with the targets.

The clarity comes in the form of the clear, tangible evidence or feedback you are giving... The empathy takes the form of listening, understanding, and being present to the needs of all involved... The investment is how you will walk alongside others.
We don't move forward by throwing hard truths at tired people. We lead them by opening our hands, inviting them to look closer, and building together.
